sourceReview: Read bundled BSB Psalm 83 in full with each verse's related passages before drafting. References are thematic or literary comparisons, not an invented historical occasion. Scripture is never stored in the notes; it loads from the bundled BSB.

study.title: Be not silent, O God
study.intro: Asaph prays as a coalition of nations plots to wipe Israel off the map, asking God to act as He did in the days of the judges so that the nations will learn that He alone is Most High.
study.context: Psalm 83 is headed 'A song. A Psalm of Asaph.' It is the last of the Asaph psalms in Book III and a community lament. Ten peoples surround Israel in an alliance, and their goal is not merely conquest but erasure. The psalmist recalls Gideon's victory over Midian and Deborah and Barak's victory over Sisera (Judges 4-8). The harsh requests are bounded by a striking purpose in verses 16 and 18: that the enemies may seek God's name and know that the LORD alone rules over all the earth.
study.peopleNote: The heading names Asaph, the Levite worship leader appointed by David; the app has no Asaph profile yet. The psalm recalls Gideon, Deborah and Barak from Judges, who also have no profiles yet. Planned paintings would show tents, armies, storms and fields; God is never portrayed as a human body.

verses.title: Do not keep still
verses.heading: A plea to a quiet heaven
verses.meaning: The heading names this a song and a psalm of Asaph. Then come three urgent requests in a row: 'O God, be not silent; be not speechless; be not still.' The psalmist feels that heaven has gone quiet while danger grows. Rather than giving up, he presses God to speak and act. Repeating the plea three ways shows how desperate the moment is. Honest prayer can tell God that His silence is hard to bear, while still trusting that He hears.
verses.context: Psalm 28:1 begs, 'Do not be deaf to me. For if You remain silent, I will be like those descending to the Pit.' Isaiah 62:6-7 calls watchmen to give God no rest until He acts for Jerusalem. Habakkuk 1:2 asks how long the prophet must cry for help.
explore: Be not silent
A request that God would no longer hold back His word or action but would speak up in judgment and rescue.
Asaph
A Levite singer appointed by David; twelve psalms carry his name, often used by his family of temple musicians.
verses.reflect: When God seems quiet, what would it look like for you to keep praying honestly instead of pulling away?
verses.alt: A lone figure kneels on a hilltop under a vast, still evening sky.

verses.title: Your enemies rage
verses.heading: Rising heads and roaring noise
verses.meaning: Verse 2 points God to the danger: 'See how Your enemies rage, how Your foes have reared their heads.' The psalmist calls them God's enemies, not just Israel's. Their noise is like a roaring crowd or a stormy sea. To 'rear the head' is to rise up in proud defiance, ready to strike. The prayer frames the crisis as a challenge to God's own honor, which gives the request weight: the conflict is ultimately with Him.
verses.context: Psalm 2:1-2 asks why the nations rage and the kings of the earth take their stand against the LORD and His Anointed. Psalm 46:6 says nations rage and kingdoms crumble when God lifts His voice. Judges 8:28 says Midian 'did not raise its head again' after Gideon.
explore: Rage
To make a loud uproar, like the roar of crowds or rough waters, expressing hostile excitement.
Reared their heads
A picture of pride and readiness to attack, the opposite of a humbled enemy whose head is bowed.
verses.reflect: How does it change your view of opposition to remember that God takes the attacks on His people personally?
verses.alt: Crowds of soldiers gather on a distant ridge, banners raised against a darkening sky.

verses.title: Secret plots
verses.heading: Scheming against God's treasured ones
verses.meaning: Verse 3 reveals the method: 'With cunning they scheme against Your people and conspire against those You cherish.' The danger is not only open warfare but crafty planning behind closed doors. Yet the verse also comforts: God's people are 'those You cherish,' literally His hidden or treasured ones. What enemies plot in secret, God sees, and those they target are kept close to His heart.
verses.context: Psalm 27:5 says that in the day of trouble God will hide His people in His shelter. Psalm 31:20 says God hides them in the secret place of His presence from the schemes of men. Exodus 19:5 calls Israel God's treasured possession.
explore: Cunning
Crafty, shrewd planning meant to trap or deceive, here aimed at destroying God's people.
Those You cherish
Literally 'Your hidden ones,' people God protects and treasures as His own possession.
verses.reflect: Where do you need to remember that you are one of God's treasured, hidden ones?
verses.alt: Shadowed men whisper together inside a dim tent lit by a single oil lamp.

verses.title: Erase the name
verses.heading: A plan to wipe out a people
verses.meaning: Verse 4 quotes the enemies: 'Come, let us erase them as a nation; may the name of Israel be remembered no more.' Their goal is total erasure, not just victory. They want Israel's very memory gone. Scripture records several such attempts, from Pharaoh to Haman, and each time God preserved His people. The psalm brings this terrifying threat into the open before God, trusting His promise to keep the line through which blessing would come.
verses.context: Esther 3:6 records Haman's plot to destroy all the Jews in the kingdom. Exodus 1:22 tells of Pharaoh's order to throw Hebrew baby boys into the Nile. Jeremiah 31:35-36 promises Israel will not cease as a nation before God.
explore: Erase as a nation
To cut off completely so that a people no longer exists as an independent group.
Remembered no more
Total forgetting of a name, which in Israel meant the loss of identity and inheritance.
verses.reflect: When you feel threatened or forgotten, how can God's faithfulness to Israel through history encourage you?
verses.alt: An old stone marker with a carved name stands half hidden by blowing desert sand.

verses.title: One mind against God
verses.heading: An alliance aimed at heaven
verses.meaning: Verse 5 says, 'For with one mind they plot together; they form an alliance against You.' Old rivals have united, putting aside their own disputes to share a common hatred. The deeper truth is in the last words: their covenant is 'against You.' Opposing God's people is opposing God. Unity is good only when it serves what is right; here, agreement becomes a tool of rebellion against the LORD.
verses.context: Psalm 2:2 says the rulers take counsel together against the LORD and His Anointed. Acts 4:25-27 applies this to the alliance against Jesus. Isaiah 8:9-10 says the nations may devise plans, but they will be thwarted, for God is with us.
explore: One mind
Literally 'one heart,' a shared intention binding the allies together in their plot.
Alliance
Literally 'covenant,' a formal pact, here made in rebellion rather than faithfulness.
verses.reflect: What does this verse teach you about choosing carefully whom you align yourself with?
verses.alt: Several chieftains clasp hands over a low stone table in a torchlit war tent.

verses.title: Edom, Ishmael, Moab, Hagar
verses.heading: Neighbors from the south and east
verses.meaning: Verse 6 begins naming the allies: 'the tents of Edom and the Ishmaelites, of Moab and the Hagrites.' Many of these were relatives of Israel. Edom came from Esau, Jacob's brother; the Ishmaelites and Hagrites traced back to Abraham's son Ishmael and his mother Hagar; Moab descended from Lot. The painful irony is that family has turned against family. 'Tents' suggests tribes and clans, many of them desert peoples.
verses.context: Genesis 36:1 identifies Esau as Edom. Genesis 25:12-18 lists the descendants of Ishmael. Genesis 19:37 records Moab's birth from Lot's elder daughter. 1 Chronicles 5:10 tells of Israel fighting the Hagrites east of Gilead.
explore: Edom
The nation descended from Esau, south of the Dead Sea, often hostile to Israel.
Hagrites
A desert tribe east of the Jordan, probably connected with Hagar, Abraham's servant.
verses.reflect: Have you ever felt opposed by people close to you, and how can you bring that hurt to God?
verses.alt: Black goat-hair tents dot a reddish desert plain beneath rocky hills.

verses.title: Gebal, Ammon, Amalek, Philistia, Tyre
verses.heading: Enemies on every side
verses.meaning: Verse 7 continues the list: 'of Gebal, Ammon, and Amalek, of Philistia with the people of Tyre.' Now the circle closes. Gebal and Ammon lay east and southeast, Amalek roamed the southern desert, Philistia held the coast to the west, and Tyre stood to the north. Israel is surrounded. Naming each enemy helps the psalmist lay the whole threat before God; nothing is hidden or minimized.
verses.context: Exodus 17:8-16 tells of Amalek's attack on Israel in the wilderness. 1 Samuel 13:5 describes the Philistines gathering a vast army. Ezekiel 27:9 mentions the elders of Gebal as craftsmen of Tyre.
explore: Gebal
Either a region south of the Dead Sea near Edom or the Phoenician city later called Byblos.
Tyre
A wealthy Phoenician port city on the Mediterranean, famous for its trade and sea power.
verses.reflect: What helps you name your troubles honestly before God instead of ignoring or exaggerating them?
verses.alt: A map-like view of hills, coast and desert, with distant camps ringing a small land.

verses.title: Even Assyria
verses.heading: A great power backs the plot
verses.meaning: Verse 8 adds a heavy weight: 'Even Assyria has joined them, lending strength to the sons of Lot.' Assyria was a growing empire from the far northeast. Its support gives the smaller nations, here Moab and Ammon (the sons of Lot), real muscle. The word 'even' shows the shock: the threat has gone international. 'Selah' invites a pause to feel the size of the danger before the psalm turns to God's past victories.
verses.context: Genesis 19:36-38 tells how Moab and Ammon descended from Lot. Deuteronomy 2:9 and 2:19 say God gave them their own lands. 2 Kings 15:19 records an early Assyrian king coming against Israel.
explore: Assyria
A powerful Mesopotamian empire, centered on the Tigris, that later destroyed the northern kingdom of Israel.
Selah
A musical or liturgical marker in the Psalms, often taken as a call to pause and reflect.
verses.reflect: When the odds look overwhelming, how can pausing to reflect help you turn toward God?
verses.alt: A long column of armored chariots rolls across a dusty plain toward the west.

verses.title: As You did to Midian
verses.heading: Remembering victories in Judges
verses.meaning: Verse 9 turns from danger to memory: 'Do to them as You did to Midian, as to Sisera and Jabin at the River Kishon.' Asaph recalls two famous rescues. Gideon's tiny band routed Midian's vast army, and Deborah and Barak defeated Sisera, Jabin's general, when the Kishon flooded. Remembering what God has done gives courage to ask Him to do it again. Past faithfulness becomes fuel for present prayer.
verses.context: Judges 7:19-22 tells how Gideon's three hundred men threw Midian into confusion. Judges 4:15 says the LORD routed Sisera before Barak. Judges 5:21 sings that 'the River Kishon swept them away.'
explore: Midian
A desert people who oppressed Israel for seven years until God used Gideon to defeat them.
Sisera and Jabin
Jabin was a Canaanite king; Sisera commanded his army of iron chariots against Israel.
verses.reflect: What past act of God's faithfulness in your life could you remember when you pray today?
verses.alt: A swollen river rushes through a valley, overturned chariot wheels caught on its banks.

verses.title: Perished at Endor
verses.heading: The end of the proud
verses.meaning: Verse 10 completes the memory: they 'perished at Endor and became like dung on the ground.' Endor lay near the battlefield where Sisera's forces fled. The image is blunt: the army that seemed unstoppable ended as refuse spread on fields. Scripture does not soften the outcome of arrogant rebellion against God. The point is that human might, however frightening, is fragile before the LORD.
verses.context: Joshua 17:11 lists Endor among the towns near the Jezreel Valley. Jeremiah 8:2 and 9:22 use the same image of dead bodies like dung on the ground. Isaiah 40:23-24 says God brings princes to nothing.
explore: Endor
A town near Mount Tabor and the Jezreel Valley, close to where Barak defeated Sisera.
Like dung on the ground
A stark image of complete disgrace and decay, bodies left unburied as worthless refuse.
verses.reflect: What fears loom large in your life that might look small in light of God's power?
verses.alt: An empty valley at dawn, broken spears and shields scattered across trampled grass.

verses.title: Oreb, Zeeb, Zebah, Zalmunna
verses.heading: Fallen princes of Midian
verses.meaning: Verse 11 names leaders: 'Make their nobles like Oreb and Zeeb, and all their princes like Zebah and Zalmunna.' These were Midian's commanders and kings captured and killed in Gideon's campaign. Oreb means 'raven' and Zeeb means 'wolf,' fierce names that did not save them. The psalmist asks that today's arrogant leaders meet a similar end, unable to carry out their plans against God's people.
verses.context: Judges 7:25 tells how Oreb and Zeeb were killed at the rock of Oreb and the winepress of Zeeb. Judges 8:21 records the end of Zebah and Zalmunna. Isaiah 10:26 recalls 'the slaughter of Midian at the rock of Oreb.'
explore: Oreb and Zeeb
Two Midianite commanders whose names mean 'raven' and 'wolf,' captured by the men of Ephraim.
Zebah and Zalmunna
Two kings of Midian pursued and captured by Gideon east of the Jordan.
verses.reflect: How does God's record of humbling the proud encourage you to stay humble yourself?
verses.alt: A rough rock outcrop and an old stone winepress stand beside a quiet valley road.

verses.title: The pastures of God
verses.heading: Coveting what belongs to the LORD
verses.meaning: Verse 12 recalls the enemy's boast: 'Let us possess for ourselves the pastures of God.' They wanted to seize the land God had given to His people. The phrase 'pastures of God' reminds them, and us, that the land was His before it was Israel's. Grabbing it was not just theft from a neighbor but trespass on God's own property. Greed that ignores God's ownership always overreaches.
verses.context: Leviticus 25:23 says, 'The land is Mine, and you are but foreigners and residents with Me.' 2 Chronicles 20:10-11 tells of Moab and Ammon coming to drive Judah out of God's possession. Psalm 24:1 says the earth is the LORD's.
explore: Possess
To take over and occupy as an inheritance, here by force against God's gift.
Pastures of God
Grazing lands and dwellings belonging to God, which He granted to Israel as their home.
verses.reflect: What in your life do you treat as yours alone that really belongs to God?
verses.alt: Green hillside pastures with grazing flocks stretch beneath a soft morning sky.

verses.title: Tumbleweed and chaff
verses.heading: Blown away by the wind
verses.meaning: Verse 13 brings nature images: 'Make them like tumbleweed, O my God, like chaff before the wind.' The plants that dry and roll across the plain, and the husks blown off the threshing floor, have no weight and no roots. The prayer asks God to scatter the allies so they cannot hold together. Note the personal address, 'O my God'; this is not a distant curse but a trusting appeal.
verses.context: Psalm 1:4 says the wicked are like chaff that the wind drives away. Isaiah 17:13 pictures nations chased like chaff and tumbleweed before a gale. Matthew 3:12 speaks of the chaff burned with unquenchable fire.
explore: Tumbleweed
Literally a whirling thing, perhaps dried thistle heads that roll across fields in the wind.
Chaff
The light husks separated from grain at threshing and carried away by the breeze.
verses.reflect: What gives your life weight and roots, so that you are not blown about by every wind?
verses.alt: Dry thistles tumble across a windswept plain while chaff drifts from a threshing floor.

verses.title: Forest fire
verses.heading: A flame racing up the mountains
verses.meaning: Verse 14 widens the picture: 'As fire consumes a forest, as a flame sets the mountains ablaze.' Wildfire in dry hills spreads with speed and power nobody can stop. The psalmist uses it to picture God's judgment overtaking enemies who thought themselves secure. The image is meant to awe us: God's holiness is not tame, and those who defy Him cannot outrun it.
verses.context: Isaiah 9:18 says wickedness burns like a fire that consumes the forest thickets. Deuteronomy 32:22 speaks of a fire kindled by God's anger that sets the mountains ablaze. Hebrews 12:29 says, 'Our God is a consuming fire.'
explore: Consumes
Eats up or devours completely, used of fire burning away everything in its path.
Ablaze
Set on fire, here pictured as flames climbing the slopes of the mountains.
verses.reflect: How does seeing God's holiness as powerful, not tame, deepen your reverence for Him?
verses.alt: Orange flames climb a forested mountainside under a smoky evening sky.

verses.title: Your tempest
verses.heading: Pursued by the storm
verses.meaning: Verse 15 continues: 'so pursue them with Your tempest, and terrify them with Your storm.' The prayer asks God to chase the enemies with a storm, the way He sent rain to flood the Kishon against Sisera. Weather in Scripture often shows God's power over creation. The goal is that their confidence melt into fear, so that they abandon their attack on God's people.
verses.context: Judges 5:20-21 sings that the stars fought from heaven and the Kishon swept the enemy away. Nahum 1:3 says the LORD's way is in the whirlwind and the storm. Job 38:1 tells of God answering Job out of the whirlwind.
explore: Tempest
A violent windstorm, used in Scripture as an instrument of God's judgment.
Pursue
To chase after relentlessly, as a warrior runs down a fleeing army.
verses.reflect: Where have you seen God's power in creation remind you that He is in control?
verses.alt: Dark storm clouds sweep across a plain as rain lashes fleeing horsemen.

verses.title: That they may seek You
verses.heading: Shame that leads to God
verses.meaning: Verse 16 reveals a hope beneath the harsh words: 'Cover their faces with shame, that they may seek Your name, O LORD.' The purpose of judgment here is not only to stop the enemies but to turn them toward God. Shame can expose pride and open the way to repentance. Even in a prayer against enemies, Asaph leaves a door open for them to come to the LORD.
verses.context: Isaiah 26:9 says that when God's judgments come upon the earth, its people learn righteousness. Jonah 3:5-10 tells how Nineveh repented and God relented. Matthew 5:44 calls believers to pray for those who persecute them.
explore: Shame
Disgrace that exposes pride, here meant to lead the guilty toward humility before God.
Seek Your name
To turn to God, calling on Him and desiring to know Him as He has revealed Himself.
verses.reflect: How might you pray for someone who opposes you, asking that they come to know God?
verses.alt: A defeated warrior sits alone beside a road, head bowed, a broken sword at his feet.

verses.title: Ever ashamed
verses.heading: Disgrace that will not lift
verses.meaning: Verse 17 asks, 'May they be ever ashamed and terrified; may they perish in disgrace.' For those who refuse to turn, the psalmist asks that their plans end in lasting failure. This is honest language about justice: evil that seeks to destroy a people must be stopped. The verse leaves the outcome in God's hands; Asaph does not take vengeance himself but asks God to deal with it.
verses.context: Romans 12:19 says, 'Do not avenge yourselves... for it is written: Vengeance is Mine; I will repay, says the Lord.' Psalm 35:4 prays that those who seek one's life be disgraced. Psalm 6:10 asks that enemies be ashamed and dismayed.
explore: Terrified
Struck with dismay and panic, the opposite of the confident pride they once had.
Perish in disgrace
To come to ruin with dishonor, their schemes collapsing and their reputation lost.
verses.reflect: What injustice do you need to hand over to God rather than seeking to settle it yourself?
verses.alt: Empty enemy tents flap in the wind on a deserted hillside at dusk.

verses.title: You alone are Most High
verses.heading: Every nation will know
verses.meaning: Verse 18 states the final goal: 'May they know that You alone, whose name is the LORD, are Most High over all the earth.' The whole psalm aims here. More than Israel's safety, Asaph wants God's name known. 'The LORD' renders God's covenant name, and 'Most High' declares His supremacy over every power. Every alliance against Him will end with this truth plain to all nations.
verses.contextTitle: The LORD over all the earth
verses.context: Exodus 6:3 records God revealing His name, the LORD, to Moses. Isaiah 45:22-23 says every knee will bow to Him. Philippians 2:10-11 says every tongue will confess that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.
explore: The LORD
Small capitals render God's personal covenant name, YHWH, revealed to Moses at the burning bush.
Most High
A title, Elyon, proclaiming that God rules above every other ruler, power or so-called god.
verses.reflect: How does knowing God is Most High over all the earth shape your hopes for the world?
verses.alt: Sunlight breaks over a wide landscape of mountains, seas and distant cities.
